title: [GDN] GDN Prefill kernel for SM100
body_opening:
## Purpose

This PR adds an in-tree GDN prefill kernel for SM100. The kernel was originally developed by team CUDA_ERROR_UNKNOWN (@simveit, @yue-zhang-2025, @mayankagarwals, @zcnrex) for  MLSys 2026 FlashInfer Kernel competition in CUDA C++. I ported the kernel to CuteDSL to enjoy JIT benefits like adaptation to various head configurations and ease of development.

This kernel requires explicit opt-in. The default backend is still FlashInfer.

### Kernel design

The kernels follow the design of FLA:
1. `kkt_inv_uw_kernel`: fusion of FLA's `chunk_scaled_dot_kkt_fwd()`, `solve_tril()`, and `recompute_w_u_fwd()`
2. `h_kernel`: FLA's `chunk_gated_delta_rule_fwd_h()`
3. `o_kernel`: FLA

The fused QK-norm + RoPE and fused LayerNorm + modulate kernels were previously gated to CUDA only. This PR enables these fused paths on ROCm, giving FLUX.2 the same eager-mode optimizations on AMD GPUs that already exist on NVIDIA.

title: perf: sort prefill requests by lora_id in scheduler
body_opening:
## Motivation

When multiple LoRA adapters are used, requests arrive interleaved (e.g., `[v1, v2, v3, v4, v1, v2, ...]`). The torch-native backend uses `torch.unique_consecutive` to merge segments, but since requests aren't grouped by adapter, each request becomes its own segment — resulting in one GEMM per request instead of one per unique adapter.

torch-native backend works better than csgmv for prefill (embeddings) with LoRA 

## Modifications

Add `--lora-sort-by-adapter` server arg (default off). When enabled, the scheduler sorts prefill requests by `lora_id` before batch construction. Since all downstream metadata is built from the sorted list, tokens arrive naturally grouped

## Title

Optimize DFlash context KV cache updates

## Summary

title: [diffusion] optimization: transfer mapped layers through a courier thread
body_opening:
A copy whose source is a checkpoint mapping is synchronous however it is requested — the driver stages unpinned memory through its own buffer — and the prefetch hooks run on the compute thread, so every mapped layer stalled the denoise step for its whole transfer. This adds a courier: a worker thread that stages a mapped layer's bytes into one of two pinned slots (a plain memcpy when the page cache holds them) and issues the device copy on its own stream, where it is genuinely asynchronous. Parameters are still rebound on the compute thread at collect time, so module state is never touched concurrently; blocking callers and any courier failure keep the direct synchronous path.

title: [V1][Perf] Cap detokenizer prompt-prime window for long prompts
body_opening:
## Purpose

- `FastIncrementalDetokenizer` primes the `tokenizers` `DecodeStream` with the entire prompt (`DecodeStream(ids=request.prompt_token_ids)`). Priming is O(prompt_len) and runs lazily on the first output token's decode step, so for very long prompts it dominates first-token detokenization latency. Incremental decoding of output tokens only needs a short trailing window of prompt context, so this PR caps the primed ids to the last MAX_PROMPT_PRIME_TOKENS (128).

- The value of MAX_PROMPT_PRIME_TOKENS, 128, is a large-enough magic number for any BPE-merge / multi-byte span.
- On DeepSeek-V4-Flash (vocab ~129k), a 998k-token prompt: the first decode step drops from ~386 ms to ~0.
